 Nearly 20,000 NES customers face power shutoffs as Nashville-area energy assistance funds run low
 NES says 19,201 accounts have a disconnect trigger date between Nov. 12 and Dec. 10, with customers owing a combined $5.1 million in overdue bills. 
 Prev 
 Next 
 Nearly 20,000 NES customers face power shutoffs as federal LIHEAP funding falls short, leaving families with few options this winter. 
 By: 
 Hannah McDonald 
 Posted 
 and last updated 
 Share Copy link Facebook Nextdoor X Threads Reddit LinkedIn Email WhatsApp Messenger Print 
 Add News Channel 5 as a Google Preferred Source 
 NASHVILLE, Tenn. (WTVF) — Time is running out for nearly 20,000 Nashville Electric Service customers who could have their power shut off, and for some, that time has already passed.
 NES executives gave their most detailed look yet at how many customers are struggling to keep their power on at their monthly board meeting Wednesday.
 As of Nov. 12, 19,201 accounts had a disconnect trigger date between Nov. 12 and Dec. 10. The largest number of customers could be affected right after Thanksgiving, between Nov. 30 and Dec. 10.
 NewsChannel 5 
 As of November 12, more than 19,200 NES customers had dates that could trigger power disconnection between November 12 and December 10. Nearly 17,000 of those accounts are in Davidson County, and more than 8,600 have fallen behind on long-term payment arrangements. NES emphasizes that a trigger date does not necessarily mean power will be shut off. 
 Customers behind on their bills owe a combined $5.1 million. As another winter approaches, some families are still trying to recover financially from last winter's ice storm.
 For two days this week, NES teamed up with the Metro Action Commission to help eligible Davidson County customers apply for LIHEAP — the Low Income Home Energy Assistance Program.
 According to the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, in 2024, nearly $83 million helped roughly 118,000 Tennessee households pay their heating and cooling bills. The average household received more than $700.
 But not everyone is eligible, and the assistance isn't always available when people need it.
 To qualify for LIHEAP, customers must fall within certain income limits, which vary by family size. For a family of four, the limit is $63,200.
 This fall, federal funding didn't arrive as expected, leaving the Metro Action Commission with only last year's leftover money to help families in need.
 One Metro Council member raised concerns about whether it is fair to keep directing customers to assistance programs that aren't fully funded.
 "The biggest challenge that I am seeing is pointing people to systems for support that are not necessarily capable of handling, making the connection, and helping people avoid disconnect," District 7 Council Member Erin Evans said.
 It's always a good idea to circle back with Metro Action Commission , NeedLink , United Way and Mid-Cumberland Community Action Agency because funding can change and/or become available on short notice.
 If you're in a position to help, Project HELP lets NES customers add a specific dollar amount to their monthly bill for temporary utility-bill assistance. You can sign up through NeedLink.
 Have you struggled to get access to home energy bill assistance? Email me at HannahCanHelp@NewsChannel5.com .
